Action Plan:
1. Acute headache management (probable migraine): treat with stronger analgesia as discussed — options offered included naproxen, paracetamol, and codeine; ibuprofen dosing advice provided (doctor stated ibuprofen may be taken up to 2 tablets three times daily). Specific prescription given/not documented in the transcript (medication name(s) and dose/route/frequency not clearly documented). Start analgesia today as discussed and reassess.
2. Symptom monitoring and safety-netting: keep a headache diary; return for review in 1–2 weeks; return earlier or seek urgent care if headaches worsen, new focal neurologic symptoms (weakness, speech change), new or progressive vision loss, persistent vomiting, fever, or if generally unwell.
3. Eye care and workplace measures: reduce screen brightness as already trialed; arrange a repeat eye test (optometry) if symptoms persist or vision/eye strain continues.
4. Secondary prevention / referral if recurrent: if headaches become frequent, consider discussion of prophylactic headache medications and possible neurology referral at follow-up.
5. Documentation/consent: Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: 3-day history of severe headache, main concern this afternoon.
- Onset/duration/progression: onset ~3 days ago at work, gradual onset, progressive/worse over the 3 days.
- Location/quality/severity: diffuse but mainly around the right eye; dull with intermittent sharper episodes; severity reported 8/10.
- Pattern/triggers/relieving factors: constant with fluctuating intensity; worse with bright light/screen exposure; reducing screen brightness provides some relief.
- Associated symptoms: photophobia ("light hurts"), transient "shooting lights" at onset (visual phenomena), feeling nauseated but no vomiting, difficulty focusing. No neck stiffness, no speech disturbance, no weakness, no recent head injury, no fever or rash.
- Past medical history: patient reports being otherwise fit and well; no chronic illnesses documented.
- Headache history: prior headaches described but not diagnosed as migraine; prior headaches previously responded to ibuprofen.
- Family history: mother and sister have frequent migraines.
- Medications: no regular medications. Patient has taken ibuprofen for the last two days (~three tablets per day as reported). (Ibuprofen dosing use in chart: doctor advised up to 2 tablets three times daily.)
- Allergies: none reported.
- Social history: works in IT (prolonged computer use); wears glasses since childhood; lives with housemates; social smoker and social alcohol use.
- Reproductive/contraception: asked about oral contraceptive use but answer not clearly documented (contraceptive status unclear).

Objective:
- No vital signs or formal physical examination findings documented in transcript.
- Neurologic review by history: no focal neurological deficits reported (no weakness, no speech disturbance, no vision loss); patient denies neck stiffness.
- Other exam findings: none recorded.
- Investigations: none performed or documented.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Headache:
   - Assessment: Migraine headache (probable acute migraine). (DDx: "Migraine headache (probable acute migraine)" — likelihood: High.)
   - Differential diagnosis (consistent with transcript and DDx):
     - Tension-type headache / stress-related headache (DDx likelihood: Medium). Supporting: dull diffuse pain, IT work, stress, improves somewhat with reduced screen brightness. Opposing: photophobia, visual phenomena, nausea favor migraine.
     - Eyestrain / computer vision syndrome (DDx likelihood: Medium-Low). Supporting: prolonged screen use, glasses long-standing, reduced brightness helps. Opposing: shooting lights and nausea less typical.
     - Acute sinusitis (DDx likelihood: Low). Supporting: periorbital pain location. Opposing: no nasal symptoms, no fever, purulent discharge not reported.
     - Intracranial mass / other serious intracranial process (DDx likelihood: Low). Supporting: progressive headache and difficulty focusing could raise remote concern. Opposing: short 3-day course, no focal neurologic signs, no red-flag features in history.
   - Investigations planned: none today. Plan to perform or arrange urgent imaging and/or urgent review if red-flag features develop (new focal deficits, vision loss, sudden severe/thunderclap headache, persistent vomiting, fever, or worsening level of consciousness).
   - Treatment planned:
     - Analgesia options discussed: naproxen (mentioned), paracetamol (mentioned), codeine (mentioned). (For naproxen/paracetamol/codeine: dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript.)
     - Ibuprofen dosing advice provided by clinician: may take up to 2 tablets three times daily (as stated in visit). Patient-reported prior ibuprofen use ~3 tablets/day; clinician advised optimizing dosing or switching agents.
     - Headache diary recommended to identify triggers and frequency.
   - Referrals: consider neurology referral and discussion of prophylactic therapy if headaches become frequent (to be considered at follow-up).

2. Vision / Eye strain (work-related):
   - Assessment: Eyestrain / computer vision–related headache (possible contributor). (DDx: "Eyestrain / computer vision syndrome" — likelihood: Medium-Low.)
   - Differential diagnosis: refractive error change; migraine with prominent visual symptoms (overlap).
   - Investigations planned: arrange/refer for an optometry/eye examination (repeat eye test).
   - Treatment planned: workplace adjustments (reduce screen brightness — already trialed), consider updated corrective lenses if indicated after eye test.
   - Referrals: optometrist/ophthalmology if eye test abnormal or symptoms persist despite adjustments.

3. Preventive care / follow-up:
   - Assessment: Risk of recurrent migraine given family history; prophylaxis not indicated today but to be considered if episodes recur/frequent.
   - Investigations planned: none specific today.
   - Treatment/referrals planned: discuss prophylactic options at follow-up; consider neurology referral if recurrent or refractory.

Quality checks
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No documented vital signs (BP, pulse, temperature).
  - No formal neurologic or focused cranial nerve / fundoscopic / eye exam recorded.
  - No documented pregnancy status or clarifying discussion about contraception (important before prescribing NSAIDs/other medications in women of reproductive age).
  - No formal documentation of which medication(s) were actually prescribed today (if any) including dose/route/frequency.
  - No baseline visual acuity/refraction or recent optometry visit details.
  - No tobacco/alcohol consumption quantities documented.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None noted; DDx items used are consistent with the transcript's history and clinician impression (migraine most likely). (If any specific red-flag diagnosis becomes suspected on later review—e.g., sudden severe onset suggesting SAH—urgent reassessment and imaging would be required.)
- Transcript quality:
  - Audio/transcript intelligible; occasional filler words but clinical history clear. Some items not fully documented (contraception status, whether prescription was provided and medication dosing).
